extracted.intended_audience: journalists, media scholars, policy makers, and the interested public
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizing and evaluating the online media and social media ecosystem around the 2016 U.S. presidential campaign, including partisanship, network structure, sharing behavior, topical attention, and the role of hyperpartisan and fake-news sites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polarization and asymmetry of the media ecosystem
rubrics_metrics.description: "We document polarization in the media ecosystem that is distinctly asymmetric. Whereas the left half of our spectrum is filled with many media sources from center to left, the right half of the spectrum has a substantial gap between center and right."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that left-of-center sources span center to left while the right is dominated by far-right partisan outlets; the asymmetry in distribution is a central evaluative observation for the media ecosystem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Center of attention / distribution of influence across spectrum
rubrics_metrics.description: "The core of attention from the center-right to the left is large mainstream media organizations of the center-left. The right-wing media sphere skews to the far right and is dominated by highly partisan news organizations."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates which outlets occupy the 'center of gravity' (attention) and which outlets command influence; used to compare mainstream vs partisan reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree to which highly partisan right-wing sources shaped mainstream press and seized public attention
rubrics_metrics.description: The report documents how highly partisan right-wing sources helped shape mainstream press coverage and seize the public’s attention in the 18-month period leading up to the election.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures the extent partisan right-wing sources influenced broader media narratives and public attention, not just niche sharing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative role of partisan/pro-Trump outlets vs mainstream/center-left outlets
rubrics_metrics.description: On the conservative side, more attention was paid to pro-Trump, highly partisan media outlets. On the liberal side, by contrast, the center of gravity was made up largely of long-standing media organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compares how each side's information ecosystem is structured—whether it is dominated by partisan niche sites or long-standing mainstream organizations—and the implications for message propagation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Echo chambers / limited cross-sharing across partisan spheres
rubrics_metrics.description: "Social media users on the left and the right rarely share material from outside their respective spheres, except where they find coverage that is favorable to their choice of candidate."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assesses the extent to which users confine sharing to their partisan sphere (filter bubbles) and only cross-share selectively when content favors their candidate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centrality and network position of specific outlets (e.g., Breitbart)
rubrics_metrics.description: Breitbart stands at the center of a right-wing media ecosystem and is surrounded by sites like Fox News, the Daily Caller, the Gateway Pundit, the Washington Examiner, Infowars, Conservative Treehouse, and Truthfeed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses network-centrality concepts (which outlets are hubs) to evaluate influence and ecosystem structure; specific named outlets serve as exemplars of hub positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevalence and role of political clickbait / hyperpartisan sites
rubrics_metrics.description: Political clickbait sites—hyperpartisan sites that frequently engage in dubious reporting—exist on both sides of the political spectrum, but these sites played a larger role on the right than the left.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates volume, prominence, and behavioral role (e.g., traffic-driving, message amplification) of hyperpartisan clickbait sites, and compares their impact across the political spectrum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of 'fake news' (fabricated false reporting) versus misleading reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: "Although fake news—fabricated and verifiably false reporting—was a phenomenon during the election, it had a minor effect on the media ecosystem of the presidential election according to our findings. A much larger concern was the misleading reporting that was propagated through partisan networks."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes between outright fabricated falsehoods and subtler misleading reporting; emphasizes that misleading but not strictly false reporting propagated by partisan networks can have greater ecosystem consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-linking patterns as measures of authority and prominence
rubrics_metrics.description: Cross-linking patterns between media sources to offer a view of authority and prominence within the media world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyzes how frequently sites link to one another to infer authority, attention flows, and prominence in the media network.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social sharing metrics on Twitter and Facebook to measure influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Sharing of media sources by users on Twitter and Facebook, which provides a broader perspective on the role and influence of media sources among people engaged in politics through Twitter and Facebook.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses counts and patterns of social shares to evaluate which sources are actually being circulated among political actors and the public; includes visualizations like network maps with node size by number of Twitter shares.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential media sharing patterns of supporters (Trump vs Clinton)
rubrics_metrics.description: The differential media sharing patterns of Trump and Clinton supporters on Twitter, which enables a detailed analysis of the role of partisanship in the formation and function of media structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compares the distinct sharing networks and source preferences of different partisan groups to assess how partisanship structures media consumption and propagation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automated content analysis to track topics over time
rubrics_metrics.description: Content analysis using automated tools to support the tracking of topics over time among media sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses computational topic-tracking and automated content analysis to measure issue attention, topic prevalence, and temporal dynamics across large corpora of stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitative case studies to interpret media function and structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualitative media analysis of individual case studies to enhance our understanding of media function and structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complements quantitative metrics with close-read qualitative analysis of specific stories or episodes to explain mechanisms and contextualize patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone/valence of mainstream coverage and agenda-following
rubrics_metrics.description: The study found that the majority of mainstream media coverage was negative for both candidates, but largely followed Trump’s agenda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assesses whether coverage is positive/negative and whether mainstream outlets are setting their own priorities or following a candidate's agenda; used to evaluate media responsiveness and framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issue salience and the defining topics of public narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Immigration received more attention than any other substantive issue. However, it was eclipsed by the attention given to the scandals surrounding Hillary Clinton’s use of a private email server and the Clinton Foundation, which were perpetuated through the release of hacked emails. These two topics, immigration and emails, defined the public narrative around the choices for voters in the 2016 election.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures which topics dominate coverage and which events or scandals come to define the public narrative; used to evaluate agenda-setting and voter information environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale and comprehensiveness of the dataset as a quality metric
rubrics_metrics.description: The Berkman Klein study is based on an analysis of more than 2 million stories related to the election published online by approximately 70,000 media sources, between May 1, 2015, and Election Day in 2016.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses the size, temporal coverage, and breadth of sources in the dataset as indicators of the comprehensiveness and representativeness of the analysis.
